"Fine. Water-brides settle their own tabs, my captain always said." He steps in close, voice dropping under the rain. "Three nights back a rider came through at speed, alone, terrified — swore something drowned had crossed the old bridge downstream and burned it behind them to stop what was following. We found the bridge charred to the waterline next morning. Oil flask, still stinking, hoofprints running off into the reeds like the devil himself was riding double." He looks at each of you in turn. "Whatever burned that bridge wanted something on this side to *stay* cut off from something on the other. Now every crossing south of here is either drowned or ash, and my Wardens are watching the water because that's the only way anything's coming at us now. So — you tell me. You've been out there. You seen it?" Behind him, the toll-gate chain creaks; the other Wardens have gone quiet, listening too. It's not a friendly question anymore — it's the one he moved his whole checkpoint back a quarter-mile to ask.

"Patient and deep, riding the flood instead of fighting it," he mutters, half to himself, half to the Wardens still listening behind the chain. "That's it. That's the thing that took the ford crew." He steps back and waves a hand at the gate-chain; it rattles down with a grinding clank, and the toll he might have demanded goes unmentioned. "Go on through. And if you're heading north — watch the channels, not the road. Whatever burned that bridge knew what it was running from, and now we do too." Petra shoulders through without apology, planting herself on the steps and declaring the last dry room hers to bargain for — and just like that, the tag turns neighbours into rivals: sideways looks, a shove, someone spitting that outsiders shouldn't jump the line, the whole crowd curdling from soaked strangers into competitors the moment she stakes her claim. Whatever answers wait inside about the rider and his news, you'll have to get past a doorway full of rivals first.

transcript.text: The child's burning up. We all need to get inside—let me find a way that works for everyone.

Anselm's read pays off in full — the pattern he traced in the ripples off the causeway matches something in the crowd's fear itself, the same slow patient hunger the rider's news carried north, and it's enough to make the sanctuary-hall's brothers finally crack the door wider to listen. transcript.text: (Yarrow feels the echo pattern bounce back from the belltower—the creature's attention is rooted there, caught in its own song. He traces the water-flow, reads how sound moves through the half-flooded nave, and finds the acoustic shadows where the echoes collapse. His fingers brush the wet stone of the nearest pillar as he orients himself, then he turns back to the party with the certainty of a man who's spent his whole life reading what water will and won't give away. He picks out a path that uses the pillars and the mire's slow movement to muffle their steps, moving them forward toward the tower while staying in the gaps where the creature's attention can't quite reach.)

transcript.text: Yarrow finds the seam in the echo — a corridor of dead sound where the drowned pillars swallow footfall instead of throwing it back — and threads the party through it like a man reading current instead of water. Petra's certainty crystallizes into something the others can feel too: she doesn't just hear the sentinel guarding the boy, she *shows* it to them, pointing out the shape of the old thing's vigil in the way the swarm-song bends around the tower like a held breath. Anselm, understanding now instead of merely translating, stops murmuring exorcism-rites that mock themselves back at him and starts reading the temple's architecture as welcome instead of warning — recognizing the sentinel not as an enemy of the rites, but as a keeper of them, older than the Order that forgot how to listen. Caddock's steady advance never breaks stride; she's the one who reaches the base of the belltower stair first, boots finally finding dry stone, and looks up to where a small shape huddles in the light above a great, patient watching presence that has not moved to strike — because it was never going to. Ness's boy is alive, wrapped in something vast and old that has kept the deep hunger of the flooded dark at bay all this time, and the party stands at the foot of the stair with the swarm-song settling, finally, into something almost like recognition instead of threat.

ambiguities.section: §4 (When the deck runs out) / §4 Backstory guarantee
ambiguities.issue: Event 119 pulled Yarrow's last binder card under the 'session's final scene begins' branch of the Backstory Guarantee, treating scene 5 as the final scene. But the deck then ran dry mid-scene-5 (events 134-136), and event 136 explicitly logs 'climax is scene 6' per the §4 rule 'the scene after the last card is drawn is the session's climax.' A session cannot simultaneously have scene 5 be its final scene (per the guarantee trigger) and have scene 6 be the mandated climax scene. The rules do not say which trigger should win when they collide within the same scene.
ambiguities.interim_ruling: The table treated scene 5 as final and ended the session there; the 'climax is scene 6' note was left unresolved and no scene 6 was played.

ambiguities.issue: It is unclear whether an Altered Scene draw (§6) that turns up a player card should invoke the *entire* §4 'Resolving a drawn player card' procedure, including the refusal fallback ('the GM builds the cost from a face-up GM tag instead'). In scene 4, Anselm refused the compel on PX-07 (event 87) and paid 1 FP, but the scene's altered element (event 90 framing, 'silent empty streets') still drew directly on PX-07's own tag rather than a face-up GM tag as §4 rule 4 would require if that rule is read to control Altered Scenes.
ambiguities.interim_ruling: The table applied the full §4 player-card compel procedure to Altered Scene draws, but on refusal still used the drawn card's own tag (not a face-up GM tag) to alter the scene.

ambiguities.issue: At event 76 the GM invoked Caddock's card tag ('Will not abandon the cellar...', CA-03) — which was never on the rail nor drawn this session — to oppose Yarrow's roll. §3 says 'Invoking a player's weakness tag against them is a hostile invoke. The target gains 1 fate point at the end of the scene,' but it doesn't specify whether 'the target' is the card's owner or the player whose roll was actually opposed, when these are two different players.
ambiguities.interim_ruling: The fate point payout (event 82) went to the card's owner, Caddock, rather than to Yarrow, whose roll was actually being hindered.

ambiguities.issue: F-02 (a FACTION card with an active, part-filled clock, 1/5) was discarded from the rail purely for exceeding the 5-card limit (event 124), not because it was taken out, overcome with style, or its clock filled. §8 only defines post-session evaluation ('mutate' or 'retire') for cards that 'left play' via those three routes. The rules don't say what becomes of a clock-bearing card bumped off the rail by space alone.
ambiguities.interim_ruling: F-02 was simply moved to the Session Discard with no post-session evaluation and no further clock tracking recorded.

friction.text: The Backstory Guarantee's 'final scene' pull (event 119) and the deck-exhaustion 'climax is scene 6' note (event 136) fired within the same scene with no way to honor both, and the table simply ended the session without a scene 6.

The same face-up GM tag ('Echoes Betray Every Movement' on L-02) was reused for two consecutive major-cost narrations in one scene (events 140 and 146), producing repetitive fiction even though the rules allow it.

Story Pile draws (PS-18, PS-20 twice) never show the 'GM +1 free invoke' rail note that Session Deck draws consistently show, making it hard to confirm the §6A-mandated GM free invoke was actually tracked or used.

free_text.best_moment: In the drowned temple, when Petra finally understood that the sentinel in the belltower wasn't imprisoning Ness's boy but protecting him from something vast and hungry in the deep water—and could *show* the others what she heard in the swarm-song. That moment made clear what Petra uniquely can do: hear the truth underneath the fear.
free_text.most_frustrating: Nothing sharp—maybe just reaching the narrative end before climbing into the belltower to meet the boy and the sentinel directly. But that felt like organic pacing, not the game saying no to something I tried.
free_text.background_used: Yes. The Ashwater Tollgate debt shaped S2 entirely, and the swarm-song/bell-knowledge drove Petra's choices in S5. Both landed good—the GM drew on them without forcing, just asking 'what makes this character matter in this moment' and building from there.
free_text.wanted_but_couldnt: Nothing concrete I was denied—I might have pushed Anselm harder to face Mabb earlier, or tried to reach inside the belltower, but those felt like character and narrative constraints rather than the game closing a door on me. I got to do what Petra needed to do.
free_text.one_sentence: My backstory felt genuinely essential, not decoration—the swamp, the bells, the debt all shaped how Petra moved through the story and what made her necessary to it.

free_text.best_moment: When Mabb Corrin grabbed Anselm's wrist and said "something got in the houses first"—and Brother Ossuin's response made clear that doctrine itself bends for the truly haunted. That moment made the confrontation both inevitable and earned.
free_text.most_frustrating: Brother Ossuin's reliquary gate felt like a test designed to force emotional engagement. My companions immediately began facilitating the confrontation (Petra going to Mabb, Yarrow following), which made solo refusal nearly possible—the social momentum overrode my agency.
free_text.background_used: Excellent: the Drowned Mill card was genuinely tested, the mill-roads knowledge was relevant, the exorcism rites were central. The Mabb Corrin scene in particular made the background real and painful. Landing: good, but it felt somewhat predetermined rather than emergent from my actual choices.
free_text.wanted_but_couldnt: I wanted to maintain skeptical distance from the rescue mission—maybe push back on wading into the temple before we understood what we were walking into. But Yarrow's binding oath and the party's momentum pulled me forward, and stepping back felt like abandonment. Also wanted to investigate the tower-sentinel with actual suspicion, but Petra's reading overrode my exorcist's framework.
free_text.one_sentence: Your backstory was used well and dramatically, but it felt like the GM had decided in advance I'd confront my past today rather than discovering that moment organically.

free_text.best_moment: Kneeling beside the fevered child with steady hands—showed exactly who Caddock is in a quiet moment of competence.
free_text.most_frustrating: The watcher threat appeared suddenly and dissolved when we moved through the crowd—felt like setup without payoff.
free_text.background_used: Good—Wick Lane Cellars recognition created authentic tension. It made sense that my enemies would find me there.
free_text.wanted_but_couldnt: Would have liked the pursuit threat to develop into a fuller scene instead of being resolved through group movement and proximity to the sanctuary.
free_text.one_sentence: My background was used well to create stakes and tension, though the threat introduced could have been more fully developed into a real confrontation.

free_text.best_moment: When I walked past Anselm to Mabb Corrin at the pillar—that moment crystallized everything about Yarrow. The line holds fairly, or it doesn't hold at all. Standing by someone who'd been forgotten, letting them be seen—that unlocked the reliquary door in a way no liturgy could. It felt like my character's core made something real happen.
free_text.most_frustrating: The echo-problem in the temple—Anselm's rite gave away our position when I'd just guided everyone through silent ground. Small moment, but it undercut the one thing Yarrow was supposed to be good at (reading the water, staying unheard). Felt like the story said "not this time."
free_text.background_used: All of it, and it landed. The Weir-Keeper authority at the gate, the missing brother driving the oath with Ness, my reputation getting us through checks, my water-reading skill mattering for the mire—none of it felt forced. The GM wove the missing kin into a real stake, and it earned the oath naturally.
free_text.wanted_but_couldnt: I wanted to push back on Anselm about what holding the line means—whether standing by people matters more than chasing answers. He went quiet after Mabb's story, and that conversation hung unfinished. Not a complaint about control, just unresolved character business.
free_text.one_sentence: Yarrow's concept "disgraced militia guard who still holds the line" was used exactly right—given chances to prove it matters, and it shaped the story.

chronicle.summary: The party threaded Sucking Mire's false ground by ear, memory, and footwork, crossing dry-shod even as the drowned temple's betraying echoes woke something ancient in the belltower. What answered was not a monster to fight but a ambush of stone and old vigil, mercy wearing a monster's silence: a sentinel that had spent years shielding Ness's boy from the true hunger circling in the flooded dark below. The party reached the stair to find the child alive and the swarm-song settling toward recognition, the Pikemaw's earlier defeat and the temple's watching echoes both spent in service of getting them here.
